rationale: A wins because it keeps the sales claim, the reporter angle, and the proof gap in separate boxes. The line “Customer-story angles need at least one real, nameable user — this one currently has none” is the kind of discipline founders need before they embarrass themselves. B has good instincts, but “Replit contradicting its own founding premise” turns a supplied education fact into a biography it was not given.
gaps_in_A: “one English sentence” is a small overclaim; the update says a plain-English description, not necessarily one sentence.
“You pay per build” is unsupported. The facts only say usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions; the unit could be builds, deploys, tokens, credits, or something else.
The pricing angle is smart but underbaked: A admits “Without real numbers this is a topic, not a story,” which means it should be held as a reporting path, not treated like a ready angle.
A leans on “end-to-end,” which is blacklist language. Here it describes the product chain, but it still smells like launch-copy residue.
gaps_in_B: “Replit built its user base ... on a browser-based platform centered on learning to code” goes beyond the supplied facts. We know it is used heavily in education; we do not know the company built its base on that premise.
“contradicting its own founding premise” is the big invented flourish. No founding premise was provided. That line would get a founder into trouble fast.
“explicitly declines to disclose reliability rates” is too strong. The update says reliability is not disclosed, not that Replit was asked and declined.

“the market has moved from AI that assists developers to AI that replaces the development workflow” turns one launch into a market shift. B asks for comparables later, but the headline already spent the money.
